QUITO, Ecuador--Alexandra Bravo, the prosecutor assigned to investigate U.S.
strikes on three Ecuadorian boats and the 36 survivors' subsequent accounts of
torture and kidnapping, was shot dead in the coastal city of Manta last month.
According to police, on June 14 a hitman aboard a black motorcycle opened fire
on Bravo as she and her sister were leaving a cafe at about 11 a.m. Bravo's
sister, who jumped to protect her, was also killed in the attack.

Upon arriving at the crime scene, officers say they found five 9mm shell
casings and Bravo's injured driver, but no sign of the police detail that had
been assigned to protect her. The Police Directorate, which operates entirely
under the executive branch, has launched a probe to determine if there'd been
an internal security breach.

Bravo is the 26th member of Ecuador's justice system to be assassinated since
2020 and the [second individual investigating state crimes murdered that
week](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jun/23/monika-silva-koniuszek-
ecuador-president-family-business). Besides her usual caseload of homicide and
organized crime, Bravo had been working the Fiorella, Negra Francisca, and Don
Maca cases--[a series of drone attacks on civilian fishing ships exposed by
Drop Site in April](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/rare-survivors-of-pacific-
boat-strikes). Two of the boat's crews returned home and reported being
abducted, blindfolded, and starved for eight days by American gunmen in U.S.
military uniforms aboard a U.S.-flagged patrol ship, before being abandoned in
El Salvador. The UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances endorsed the calls
for an investigation, demanding that the U.S. provide information on the
whereabouts of the eight still-missing men and any involvement in the matter
by April 27. To date, the United States has not responded.

Under Ecuador's right-wing president Daniel Noboa--[a Miami-born billionaire
often characterized as a "U.S.-backed
dictator"](https://peoplesdispatch.org/2026/04/13/ecuador-a-quasi-
dictatorship-aligned-with-the-donroe-doctrine/)--the country has become a
central testing ground for Operation Southern Spear, Washington's
extrajudicial bombing campaign purporting to target "narco-terrorists," which
has killed 221 people to date. There is no evidence that many of the victims,
including those in Bravo's investigation, had engaged in drug trafficking.

"I can't make any assertion regarding it being a political assassination, but
evidently, when a prosecutor is killed it's because of the investigation
they're conducting," Fernando Bastias, a renowned human rights attorney with
Ecuador's CDH and member of the Geneva-based World Organization Against
Torture, told Drop Site, "That's something we've learned from our experience
in Ecuador."

A source inside the Manta police department, who knew Bravo personally, told
Drop Site that the Ecuadorian prosecutor was under pressure from her superiors
at the Attorney General's office to treat the U.S. attacks as exclusively
"cases of disappearance." The source, who asked for anonymity out of fear of
retaliation, said Bravo was told to close all lines of inquiry after 36 of the
44 missing men were found--despite arriving with severe injuries, including
70% vision loss and feet torn to flesh and bone, which medical experts found
consistent with their accounts of explosions and torture.

A senior researcher with Human Rights Watch, Nathalye Cotrino Villarreal, who
interviewed Bravo as part of her investigation into the three vessels,
similarly recalled Bravo facing "internal challenges within the institution
itself to advance the investigation." Villarreal said the prosecutor
repeatedly sought cooperation from other branches responsible for the ship's
rescue, including the Manta Port Captaincy, but "none responded to her
requests for information." During the Negra Francisca bombing, Darwin Pico-
Flores, an eyewitness aboard a nearby boat, told Drop Site he called the Manta
Port Captaincy to request emergency assistance. Nobody came. In April, as part
of its first investigation into the incident, Drop Site called the port
seeking comment. Officials hung up after learning the call was from
journalists.

As of their last meeting on May 8, Cotrino Villarreal told Drop Site, Bravo
"was still in the initial stages of inquiry and investigation." Bastias said
Bravo "was investigating a country [United States] that has been positioned in
the media as an ally against crime. That investigation has not advanced at
all, and that stems from an intention to avoid getting into trouble or
problems with anyone."

The source inside the Manta Police Department said that, given this lack of
cooperation from partner agencies, Bravo had asked for advice on how to pursue
new sources for evidence.

In the days leading up to her death, Bravo was relocated to the Attorney
General's office in Montecristi, a neighboring municipality. Her caseload
changed after the transfer and she was no longer in charge of investigating
the three boat attacks. Drop Site attempted to reach Bravo's replacement for
comment but he had been explicitly instructed not to speak to the press. After
weeks of attempts to reach the Attorney General's office for comment, they
told Drop Site the investigation was sealed and they could not comment on why
Bravo was relocated.

Inside Ecuador's U.S.-backed military regime,[ the Attorney General's office
has become an increasingly opaque and politicized
institution](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/ecuador-left-us-linked-
prosecutor). "It's already a major obstacle for prosecutors to investigate
local state agents. Now imagine international state agents," Bastias said.
"The Executive Branch has implemented a series of legal frameworks that leave
these foreign state agents immune from prosecution," he added, referring to
the diplomatic immunity granted to all U.S. military and Department of Defense
personnel through President Noboa's 22 martial law decrees.

The Pentagon, Coast Guard, and U.S. Southern Command have all denied any
knowledge or responsibility of the boat incidents. After Drop Site published
photo evidence of the Negra Francisca bombing, U.S. [lawmakers questioned U.S.
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth during a congressional
hearing](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fFKEMaAjjP4). On June 13, the day
before Bravo's murder, Reps. Joaquin Castro (D-Texas) and Bill Keating
(D-Mass.) [published a letter
](https://castro.house.gov/imo/media/doc/20260611ecuadorstrikescastrokeating.pdf)to
Hegseth, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Head of the U.S. Coast Guard,
Kevin Lunday, [demanding a full audit of U.S. government involvement in the
attacks.](https://castro.house.gov/imo/media/doc/20260611ecuadorstrikescastrokeating.pdf)
Despite the deadline of July 10, none of the agencies have issued a public
response. Keating's press secretary Lauren McDermott told Drop Site that his
office had received a reply from Rubio's office, but none from the Department
of War or Coast Guard. She did not disclose the contents of the response.

The survivors who returned home, and the families of those who didn't, still
have not received any answers, telling Drop Site "authorities shut the door in
our face." Maria, the wife of one of the fishermen, tells Drop Site her
mother-in-law died awaiting her son's return, saying she was struggling with
severe depression and stopped in the weeks leading up to her death.

Despite both governments' efforts to stonewall the investigation, evidence
continues to emerge supporting the fishermen's accounts of abduction,
airstrikes, and torture. Drop Site obtained exclusive video of U.S. Coast
Guard activity in the vicinity of the Negra Francisca bombing, open-source
intelligence that corroborates the Negra Francisca's testimonies, and police
interviews with eyewitnesses that confirm the U.S. involvement alleged by
survivors and documented by Drop Site. With the help of Airwars OSINT analyst
and former U.S. Marine Corps member Tomi McCluskey, Drop Site accessed
additional NASA thermal imagery consistent with the Negra Francisca bombing
and vessel tracking data placing U.S. Coast Guard activity along the route the
fishermen say they were taken after the strike.

_Video obtained by Drop Site showing alleged Coast Guard activity near the
Negra Francisca strike._

## **Political Lawfare Under Ecuador 's U.S.-Backed Military Regime**

Noboa, who governs by military curfews and [mass starvation of political
prisoners](https://www.connectas.org/especiales/encerrados-para-morir-
carceles-ecuador/), has gone to great lengths to become Trump's strongest
partner in South America. Since taking office, he brushed aside Ecuador's
constitutional ban on U.S. military presence--ratified by 60% of voters as
recently as November 2025--which was originally introduced [almost 20 years
ago](https://www.wola.org/sites/default/files/downloadable/Andes/Ecuador/past/March%202007%20Manta%20Memo.pdf)
precisely due to a history of U.S. military sinking boats off the coast of
Manta. Additionally, his administration authorized the first FBI office on
Ecuadorian soil, assisted a [U.S. Embassy
effort](https://substack.com/home/post/p-200021648) to falsely frame members
of Colombia's left-wing government ahead of elections, and collaborated with
the U.S. in [the
bombing](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/03/24/world/americas/us-ecuador-drug-
camp-bombing-dairy-farm.html) of innocent civilian farmworkers along the
Colombian-Ecuadorian border--all in the name of combatting drug trafficking.

Notably, boats from Noboa's [family shipping
corporation](https://revistaraya.com/daniel-noboas-family-business-president-
of-ecuador-is-involved-in-cocaine-trafficking-to-europe) were caught
trafficking ₤26 million of cocaine--a detail that has not deterred the State
Department from naming him a key partner in Trump's War on Drugs. Last month,
The Guardian [reported](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/jun/23/monika-
silva-koniuszek-ecuador-president-family-business) that a whistleblower who
was investigating Noboa's ties to drug trafficking was murdered.

Still, Noboa remains a member in good standing of Trump's Shield of the
Americas. The Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, as the Shield is also known,
functions as both a military and a highly political alliance, having openly
intervened to prop up U.S. interests in Bolivia as President Rodrigo Paz faced
off with anti-austery protests.

A local prosecutor charging U.S. forces with extrajudicial bombings and
torture of Ecuadorian civilians would undermine the alliance and damage
Ecuador-U.S. relations.

Other government officials investigating U.S.-Ecuadorian criminal collusion
received death threats. Monica Palacios, a National Assembly lawmaker
representing Ecuadorians living in the United States, who announced plans to
bring the Fiorella boat case before the United Nations, faced months of
political lawfare after exposing a U.S.-Ecuadorian government embezzlement
scandal. Last Friday,[ Palacios said she received death
](https://www.instagram.com/reel/Da3Bd1IxHN-/)threats against herself and her
one-year-old son, along with footage of the outside of her New York home. She
directly blamed President Noboa, saying the threats were retaliation for her
investigation into U.S.-Ecuadorian corruption.

"There is a direct persecution of judges and prosecutors who, within the scope
of their duties, make decisions that are not entirely aligned with what the
Executive Branch wants and end up being sanctioned," Bastias, the human rights
attorney, said. "On the other hand, there is also the risk stemming from the
context of criminality." Regardless, he asserted, Bravo's death "has a lot to
do with what the state does or does not do, because so far there haven't been
any effective security mechanisms for the justice system's civil servants. The
responsibility lies in having failed to ensure protection."

Diego Vintimilla Jarrin, formerly a lawmaker with Ecuador's National Assembly
and now a spokesperson for Ecuador's Communist Party, similarly told Drop
Site, "Noboa's government is the most anti-sovereign agenda we have had since
the start of democracy. I have no proof of who murdered the prosecutor but the
fact that she was investigating certain elements and that they later ceased to
seem important also says a lot about the underlying issues."

## **New Evidence Implicating U.S. Emerges**

#### **The Negra Francisca**

The U.S. maintains it never interacted with any of the three boats. A
spokesperson for the U.S. Coast Guard told The Guardian that the agency's only
involvement in the events was deploying the USCGC Bertholf on a search-and-
rescue mission after receiving a MAYDAY alert that the Negra Francisca was on
fire, and ultimately found nothing.

But tracking data of the Bertholf's movements, provided exclusively to Drop
Site by McCluskey, places the cutter near the Negra Francisca around the time
of the bombing before turning off its signal--only to reappear off the shore
of Costa Rica the same dates the Negra Francisca crew were taken into Central
American waters and transferred to El Salvador's Naval Command, with mangled
limbs and major burn injuries from the attack. Hernan Flores, captain of the
Negra Francisca, told Drop Site that Salvadoran officers specifically informed
him that "U.S. personnel had called to coordinate the handoff."

The Coast Guard denied that it coordinated the handoff. "The Coast Guard did
not play any role in the transfer of fishermen from the Negra Francisca Duarte
II," said a spokesperson.

The USCGC Bertholf departed the Galapagos military base at 4 p.m. on March 16
and stopped transmitting its location shortly afterwards. A day later, the
Negra Francisca was bombed 170 miles away--a distance typically covered by
boat in 3 to 10 hours. Drop Site asked the U.S. Coast Guard to account for the
cutter's activity after its signal went dark. The Coast Guard responded it
"does not disclose cutter movements during law enforcement missions for
operational security."

At 1:02 p.m. on March 17, NASA FIRMS registered a thermal anomaly consistent
with an explosive fire, corroborating the time and location where Negra
Francisca fishermen told Drop Site their ship was set ablaze by multi-drone
strikes. The crew say they were then seized at gunpoint by English-speaking
men with blond hair dressed in khaki fatigues with American flag patches
stitched onto their sleeves--their descriptions match the uniforms pictured in
[U.S. Southern Command press
releases](https://www.war.gov/Multimedia/Photos/igphoto/2002833351/index.html).
Aboard the U.S.-flagged patrol ship, the gunmen allegedly held them hostage,
sank their bombed boat, placed hoods over their heads, beat some of the
fishermen, and withheld food for eight days as they transported them to
Central America.

The USCGC Bertholf's signal resurfaced in Costa Rican waters on March 22 near
the Golfito Port, approximately 450 nautical miles from El Salvador's waters.
It turned off its transponder and did not reactivate it until March 24, 24
hours after El Salvador's Coast Guard publicly announced having had the Negra
Francisca fishermen in their custody.

As part of our first investigation, Drop Site reached out to 11 government
personnel in El Salvador. All of them refused to go on the record, citing a
media gag order.

There is precedent for the Bertholf transferring victims of U.S. airstrikes to
Central American authorities, with Costa Rican outlets reporting it delivered
the remains of two deceased and one injured survivor to Costa Rica's Port of
Golfito around the same time. Costa Rica's nautical inspector Wilber Urroz
Guido said he had no information on the cutter's movements but that it was
authorized to act under a memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and
Costa Rica--similar to agreements the U.S. maintains with Ecuador and El
Salvador.

Eyewitness testimony also casts doubt on the U.S. Coast Guard's version of
events. Video footage shared exclusively with Drop Site by Darwin Flores-Pico,
an eyewitness to the attack and nephew of the Negra Francisca's captain, shows
a U.S. Coast Guard cutter patrolling the waters where the bombing occurred.

_Video obtained by Drop Site showing alleged Coast Guard activity near the
Negra Francisca strike._

Darwin said he was fishing nearby on March 17, aboard his boat the Solavil,
when he spotted smoke rising in the distance around 2 p.m. While making
repeated attempts to reach the Negra Francisca's crew by radio, he spotted an
American aircraft circling above. It wasn't until hours later that he learned
by radio signal that the Negra Francisca was in flames and rushed to make his
way to the scene, finding the vessel consumed by fire and no sign of
survivors.

He recovered two scorched emergency skiffs, took photo evidence of the fire,
then called the Port of Manta to ask for help. Nobody came.

Darwin decided to begin his journey back to the port to get emergency
assistance and, as he was leaving the scene of the fire, red and green lights
descended upon the Negra Francisca. Fearing for his safety, he steered his
boat away from the site.

The following afternoon, Darwin told Drop Site his boat was boarded by the
U.S. Coast Guard, which detained and questioned the crew for nearly 12 hours
via a Spanish translator with a Puerto Rican accent. He said Coast Guard
personnel confirmed the red and green lights were from their patrol and
acknowledged reaching the site of the _Negra Francisca_ the previous night,
but refused to elaborate on anything they'd found.

Instead, they questioned the fishermen about whether they'd seen anything and
why Darwin had salvaged the skiffs. After telling the Coast Guard officials
that the Negra Francisca was his uncle's boat, Darwin says they abruptly
stopped questioning him and began communicating by radio in English with
colleagues aboard the nearby cutter shown in the video. "Since we were the
only people who saw everything, we were afraid they might do something to us,"
Darwin said. He felt the U.S. Coast Guard showed little interest in helping
him locate his family and instead seemed more focused on "making sure we
weren't witnesses to anything."

McCluskey says the multi-drone tactic--described by all three boats--reflects
a U.S. doctrine. He argues it's unlikely that other regional powers, from
neighboring countries to organized crime groups, would have the budget or
access for such technology. There is no known precedent of cartels using "eye-
in-the-sky" surveillance drones deep in maritime territory, though the Coast
Guard has also denied operating armed drones in Ecuadorian waters.

Furthermore, the decision to keep the survivors alive, albeit involving
testimonies of torture, and the efforts and expenses to transport them, is far
more reflective of a Department of Defense protocol---designed to avoid
international legal ramifications--than any organized crime group would
typically care to practice. "If it was cartels, you would've never found
them," McCluskey said. "There would be no survivors to talk to, there would be
no stories."

#### **The Fiorella**

The Fiorella was struck off the coast of the Galapagos on January 20; all
eight fishermen aboard remain missing. The day before the vessel vanished, the
captain's wife received a call from her husband on an emergency line, warning
that U.S. aircraft were orbiting overhead.

Drop Site obtained police interview transcripts from two eyewitnesses,
Christian Flores and Dimas Ignacio Álvarez, who corroborated seeing the
Fiorella engulfed in smoke and surrounded by American assets. The two men were
members of the Fiorella crew but had been out setting a long line on a nearby
raft for several hours when the vessel went up in smoke.

In their police statements, Flores and Álvarez described two U.S. aircraft
flying over the Fiorella on January 18; multiple grey American drones and a
U.S.-flagged patrol ship circling the vessel on January 19; and, on January 20
--the day their crewmates disappeared--the large U.S.-flagged patrol ship near
the smoke. From a distance, they could not make out the personnel aboard the
ship, but their accounts echo those of the Negra Francisca crew, who said they
were taken hostage by armed Americans aboard a U.S.-flagged patrol vessel. The
witnesses' descriptions also match aircraft and equipment featured in public
posts by U.S. Southern Command.

After spotting the smoke, the two fishermen said they heard their crewmates
calling the captain over the radio in distress. They were never seen again.

The attorney representing the two survivors of the Fiorella, Juan Avila, told
Drop Site that the slain prosecutor, Alexandra Bravo, was in fact his niece.

The Coast Guard told Drop Site it "has no record of involvement with La
Fiorella."

## **Bravo Is No Anomaly**

The absence of an assigned police detail when Bravo was murdered bears
similarities to the 2023 assassination of frontrunner presidential candidate
Fernando Villavicencio. A congressional commission determined that
Villavicencio's police detail was insufficient, that he had been
unconventionally escorted through an exposed street-level exit contrary to
standard protocol, and that the armored vehicle designated to protect
Villavicencio on the campaign trail had been left by his security team in
another city that day. These breaches made him particularly vulnerable when
assailants approached and shot him on the sidewalk as he was leaving a meeting
with other government officials.

Villavicencio's death cleared the way for now-President Daniel Noboa's
campaign--[which had been polling at
3%](https://cepr.net/publications/ecuador-news-round-up-no-5-campaign-for-the-
runoff-now-underway/)--to surge to victory. In an interview with Señal
Colombia, National Assembly legislator and member of Villavicencio's party,
Gisella Molina, who was with him and injured during the assassination,
suggested government officials had prior knowledge of the plot.

During the 2024 murder investigation, Drop Site
[published](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/ecuador-left-us-linked-prosecutor)
private messages from then-Attorney General Diana Salazar revealing a plot to
implicate former democratic socialist President Correa's party in
Villavicencio's assassination, amid close collaboration with the U.S.
ambassador.

The state later concluded that the Los Lobos cartel carried out
Villavicencio's murder and alleged that former members of Correa's party were
the masterminds. Prosecutors assert that Los Lobos killed Villavicencio for
exposing their criminal network. While Villavicencio campaigned on eradicating
the cartel economy, Ecuador under Noboa--[accused of offering organized crime
bosses immunity in exchange for electoral
support](https://www.elmundo.es/cronica/2026/03/21/69b9a8c6e85ecefe738b4594.html)--has
risen as the top distribution hub for 70% of the world's cocaine.

Immediately following Bravo's death, the Attorney General issued a public
statement attributing her murder to retaliation against prosecutors combating
organized crime. When asked why authorities had linked the killing to
organized crime and whether investigators had uncovered any information about
Bravo's missing police protection detail, the Attorney General's office told
Drop Site the investigation is under seal and declined to comment.

Though the attorney general has yet to present evidence to support their
claim, Bravo lamented to the Human Rights Watch that "danger was always
present" in her work. "She said that being a prosecutor in a context of
organized crime was complex and risky, but she did not provide any further
details," Cotrino Villarreal told Drop Site. Manta sits at the epicenter of
Ecuador's organized crime crisis, as the small South American country becomes
[the most violent nation](https://responsiblestatecraft.org/ecuador-military-
noboa/) in the Western Hemisphere.

Bravo was also responsible for looking into the unsolved 2024 disappearance of
the Patricia Lynn ship and its 21 crew members.

Bravo is the second person associated with the Patricia Lynn case to be
assassinated. The first was the mother-in-law of one of the disappeared
fishermen who became the spokesperson for the victims' families and organized
marches demanding answers for their missing relatives. Maria Choez was fatally
shot by two armed assailants while operating her street food stand in downtown
Manta.

Cotrino Villarreal says the sinking of the [Patricia Lynn boat
](https://www.primicias.ec/seguridad/misteriosa-desaparicion-barco-patricia-
